title: A ladder pinned to the wrong clock

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the fifteenth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
A missile reached the one address the Houthis had spent a week promising to hit.
[thoughtful] A jury in Delaware found a breach of contract and priced it at two dollars.
Singapore handed out masks below its own published threshold. And the first computer was a loom — which you can still buy, from Norway.
[amused] Hold that one. Lead first.

Dhahran. Late on Tuesday a missile hit an administrative building inside Saudi Aramco's headquarters complex. Fifty-eight square kilometres, around eleven thousand residents, and the control room that watches the rigs, the refineries and the pipelines.
Two accounts, neither withdrawn. The Energy Ministry, through the state news agency, said the site was targeted, resulting in — their words — a limited fire. No injuries, no deaths.
[curious] And the other one?

Reuters, citing three people with direct knowledge, reported extensive damage. Two said the fire began on the ninth floor of the south wing and spread between the sixth and the tenth. A fourth said it burned into Wednesday.
Another of them said the top three floors — which hold chief executive Amin Nasser's office — were severely damaged. Ceiling partly down, windows blown out, staff sent home.
Bloomberg confirmed the strike independently and could resolve neither the damage nor whether the building took a direct hit or falling debris. So we print both accounts, and say which is which.
And Aramco's line?

Nasser said the system is intact, and twelve million barrels a day could be available within days. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree called it a high-quality military operation that will continue in the coming days.

Since the eighth of October, three thousand one hundred and twenty flights have been cancelled — about forty-one per cent of departures. Riyadh's airport is shut to the seventeenth. Across the week Bloomberg counted at least eighteen killed.
The foreign ministry advised deferring all travel to Saudi Arabia, and MUIS asked Umrah pilgrims to consider postponing — acknowledging financial implications through no fault of their own.
The Fund published its World Economic Outlook in Bangkok on Monday. The global number is deliberately dull: three point one per cent this year, three point four next, raised.
So where's the story?
The regional tables. The Middle East and North Africa contracts two per cent this year — cut by three point one points since April. The only region in the book forecast to shrink.
Which countries?
Kuwait, minus sixteen point seven. Qatar, minus fifteen point six. Iraq, minus sixteen. Saudi Arabia, minus three point three. Oman, plus four point one — the only Gulf economy still growing.
Their chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, says the economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits.

Singapore, and the rung that never came. The environment agency published a response ladder on the ninth of October. The first rung is a twenty-four-hour reading above two hundred — that's when N ninety-five masks go out.
Never. One hundred and ninety-two on the ninth was the high-water mark. On Tuesday the band ran one hundred and eighteen to one hundred and sixty-eight. The masks went out anyway.
[curious] On what basis?

A different instrument. The one-hour particulate reading reached one hundred and thirty-nine to two hundred and fifty-one micrograms per cubic metre — Band two to Band four, Very High. The top of the range roughly tripled in twenty-one hours.
Which this desk says is the right call, and an admission that the rung is wrong. A twenty-four-hour average is designed to be stable, which is another way of saying it's designed to be late.
And the Haze Act?

Still on its shelf. Neither advisory mentions it — a fortnight after the agency said the air met its trigger, and with four investigations from twenty fifteen still open. Twelve years, no completed prosecution.
Minister Grace Fu, handing out masks at Yuhua: Singapore is keeping our options open. Jakarta has given no answer to Singapore's offer of help.
The Atelier. This week, pillows and bolsters.

Start with fill power, because everyone quotes it. It's a machine reading — a ninety-four point two five gram acrylic plate dropped onto thirty grams of down in a two hundred and eighty-eight millimetre cylinder, read at sixty seconds.
How reliable?
The lab that runs the test says a result could be plus or minus five per cent of the actual fill power. And one to two per cent can equal eight to sixteen points.
[wry] So six hundred and six fifty are one shipment apart.
Transit alone costs five to twenty per cent. And nobody weighs an ounce of down into a pillow. The honest measures are oxygen number and turbidity — and nobody advertises either.
[curious] And provenance?
By the trade's own origin table, China supplies seventy-six point seven per cent of world down. Hungary, three. Poland, one.
[curious] What do owners say?
One large aggregator ranks by attribute, not brand. On one thousand nine hundred and seven reports, down scores a C for support. Buckwheat, on four thousand and ninety-one, scores an A.
Down wins on cuddliness and lightness. That's the whole list.
[curious] And here?

The standard Singapore bolster is twenty-three by ninety-one centimetres — bantal peluk in Malay. No Singapore maker could be documented. The trade survives at Sin Keng Wah in Johor Bahru, founded nineteen sixty-four, where Yeow Sien Soon, sixty-three, still hand-fills Thai kapok for the Johor royal family.
And for this climate?

Kapok can't be washed and lasts three to five years. Down needs a dehumidified bedroom. Latex is the only fill whose failure mode is unrelated to moisture — it dies of ultraviolet, which is why never dry it in sun is this market's most important care line. Heveya sells one compound in six lofts at two hundred and ninety-eight Singapore dollars.
And the expensive mistake?
Loft, not fill.

Technology. A jury in Wilmington, Delaware returned on Tuesday after five days. It found Arm breached its Architectural License Agreement with Qualcomm, and intentionally and negligently interfered with Qualcomm's relationship with Meta.
[curious] Damages?
One dollar on each count. Two dollars in all.
[laughs] Two dollars. So what was it actually about?

Not the money. Qualcomm is pursuing a clause letting it stop paying Arm royalties for five years after a breach — the thing Reuters calls worth billions. Judge Noreika has not ruled on whether it's enforceable.
And a correction from us.

Yes. The one hundred and seventy million dollars we printed in issue one thirty-two needs recasting. It was Qualcomm's claimed loss of value in a near-final Meta deal after Arm leaked a licence-termination threat — not a damages demand.
The Home Lab. A pull request that is faster and slower at the same time.

Pull request two nine two one nine adds matrix-multiply support for two quantisations in llama dot cpp. On the author's own bench, one goes from ninety-two to seven hundred and sixty-three tokens a second at one thread. Eight point three times.
And the catch?
Read his own table further down. At four threads it's one point eight times. At eight threads, one point two three.

Then on the day of the merge, the maintainer posted his own run on the same machine with a real workload — a four-billion-parameter model at four thousand tokens. Eighteen per cent slower prefill, thirty per cent slower decode.
[curious] What did the author do?

Raised no objection, approved the pull request and merged it himself the same day. Replied the next morning that the native path's showing was interesting, and offered model size and thread count as explanations — with no new measurements.
[deadpan] So both numbers are public. Only one is in the summary.
The Kit. Ray-Ban Meta Audio shipped on Tuesday, and the product is a subtraction. Open-ear speakers, six microphones, the assistant, the frames — and the camera removed.
Price?

Three hundred and forty-nine US dollars, three hundred and nineteen pounds. And nothing in Singapore — Meta's Singapore page lists it as Not available, twice on the same page, while selling three other pairs here, priced.
[skeptical] Any numbers behind the claims?
Meta calls these its lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet, and doesn't say which glasses that's measured against. Engadget weighed them: Meta's page says forty-three grams, its reviewer got forty-seven.
Both figures published. And Meta says the microphones capture your voice more clearly than earbuds — naming no earbud, no measurement and no method.
[warmly] And a win for Singapore.

The HomePod mini two. Announced Monday, and the Singapore release names the country, opens pre-orders at nine this morning, and publishes one hundred and ninety-nine Singapore dollars. Two issues ago we counted nine Apple accessories that excluded Singapore from every one.
The Good Life. Seiko has made a panda chronograph, and limited means five thousand pieces.
[amused] Five thousand, each engraved to remind you.

Each caseback carries the words LIMITED EDITION. The second reference runs to two thousand — and in seven days this desk counted ten thousand two hundred watches announced as Japanese limited editions.
[curious] Singapore price?
Seven hundred and sixty-three dollars, which is rarer than the watch. No yen price could be read at all — Seiko's Japanese page timed out and no Japanese retailer carried a figure.
[wry] Is it actually a good watch?

The design is genuinely good — the pushers are ears, the subdials are drooping eyes. But a numbered caseback on five thousand pieces is a production run with a stop date, not scarcity. The only honest reason to buy it is that you want it.
Screen and Sound. Four days before the data existed, the chart's own publisher called the result.
[skeptical] And did it?
For the week to the fifteenth, the Beatles are at number two. Blossoms won, from Stockport, with Songs from the Wedding Cake. New.
The Family Desk. A Flemish school did what Singapore did in January — extended phone restrictions from lesson time to the whole school day.
KU Leuven surveyed eight times across one academic year. Nine hundred and sixty pupils, three thousand and ninety-nine observations, the first wave before the ban.
[curious] Result?

In the short run, nothing. Social loneliness, p equals zero point seven three seven. Cyberbullying victimisation, p equals zero point nine two two. But across seven waves social loneliness rose — plus two hundredths per wave, p equals zero point zero zero two.
[curious] It went up after the phones went away.

With caveats, which are large. No control group, no pre-ban trend, one school. The loneliness scale had to be cut to two items. No correction for multiple comparisons. And phones stayed outside school hours.
Our own guidance?

Grow Well SG gives under two hours a day for ages seven to twelve outside schoolwork, and says it will be extended to older age groups subsequently. That was January twenty twenty-five, and there is still no published figure for a thirteen-year-old.
The Macro Desk. September inflation came in hot at half past eight.
[curious] How hot?
Headline up zero point six per cent on the month and three point seven on the year, against three point six expected. Core zero point three three five against zero point two.

Energy rose five point two per cent on the month. Petrol alone rose nine point one — and accounted for more than half the entire monthly rise in all items. Core is two point six per cent, barely above target.
[thoughtful] So it's the Gulf arriving in the American basket.

The policy path repriced inside the hour. The Fed raised a quarter point in September — unanimously, its first hike since twenty twenty-three. October odds roughly doubled: three sources read directly give thirty-nine point three per cent, forty-seven point one, and about fifty.
Goolsbee called the print discouraging, and four per cent annualised core not acceptable.

The two-year spiked to four point nine five and the ten-year jumped about ten basis points — before both reversed. The ten-year settled at five point one eight seven, down three. The thirty-year down three point nine.

Which tells you what broke equities that afternoon was not inflation. It was private credit. CoreWeave's twenty thirty-two bonds touched a fifteen per cent yield and closed at a record fourteen point five, against a nine point six two five coupon at issue in June.

And Singapore. Ten of ten economists polled expected MAS to tighten. It held — no change to the slope, and no change to the width of the band or the level at which it is centred. The dollar fell zero point three eight per cent.
The Rabbit Hole. This week we went down into handweaving, and came back with a thesis: the first computer was a loom, and it still ships.
[curious] Start with the mechanism.

Cloth is two sets of threads crossing at right angles. The warp runs lengthwise under tension; the weft is the thread you throw across. Everything in handweaving answers one question — how do you lift some warp threads and not others, thousands of times, without touching them?
And the answer?

The shed. The triangular tunnel that opens when some threads rise and the rest stay down. A heddle is a loop with an eye, one warp thread each. A rigid heddle is a slotted comb with two positions — plain weave and nothing else.

A shaft is a frame holding a bank of heddles, and now you can group threads arbitrarily. N shafts give two to the n possible sheds. Two is tabby. Four is the workhorse. Eight is where the community says the forever loom starts. Sixteen is damask.
And at the end of the ladder?
Every warp end gets its own hook, and there is no draft any more — only an image. That's Jacquard.
[thoughtful] Which is where the computing comes in.

Jacquard's punched-card loom stored its program on cards strung in a loop. Babbage took the idea for the Analytical Engine, and kept a silk portrait of Jacquard, woven on one, that looked like an engraving. Hollerith later used cards for data, and his company became IBM.

And the machine never stopped being made. A digital Jacquard — two hundred and twenty pneumatically controlled heddles per module, fed an image file — is built in Moss, Norway today, from thirty-eight thousand euros. A full-width sample needs twelve modules. Seventy-three thousand.
[curious] What does a person actually buy?

A Schacht Cricket at two hundred and forty-one dollars for a rigid heddle. An Ashford eight-shaft table loom at one thousand one hundred and ninety-nine. Harrisville's eight-harness floor loom, one thousand eight hundred direct from the maker in New Hampshire.
[curious] And secondhand?

This is the hobby's defining economic fact. The Weavers Guild of Rochester's used list carried a forty-eight inch eight-harness Macomber at eight hundred and fifty dollars. New equivalents start near five thousand.
Because the men who built them are dead. The used lists are full of makers whose looms are bargains for exactly that reason.
Anything new this year?

Smaller than a loom and more interesting. LoftyFiber shipped a sensor array that sits under the treadles, reads a draft off a card, and sounds a different tone the instant you press a wrong combination.
[curious] And Singapore?

One studio deep. Craft Atelier, at Centropod on Changi Road, by appointment. Multi-shaft fundamentals at four hundred dollars a day, and a ninety-dollar study group that is the closest thing the island has to a guild. There is no Singapore weaving guild.
Does the climate help or hurt?

Both. Natural fibres are hygroscopic — industrial weaving sheds are deliberately humidified. A linen warp is genuinely easier to weave here than in Colorado. But a loom is solid timber under tension, and the problem isn't the heat. It's the cycling.
[curious] Air conditioning.
It swings a room between eighty-five and fifty-five per cent twice a day. Beaters rack out of square, cords stretch, reeds pit. Put the dehumidifier near the steel, not the timber.
Fitness. The biggest study of its kind just added two points. Five hundred and sixty-two thousand adults, ten years of median follow-up.
[curious] And the headline?

A hazard ratio of zero point eight four per additional metabolic equivalent, and adjusted ten-year mortality of thirty-two point nine per cent in the least-fit quintile against thirteen point four in the fit. Enormous numbers, not in dispute.
Three things underneath. The confidence interval on that hazard ratio is four thousandths wide — which measures how large the sample is, not how accurate the estimate is.

The paper does not report the mean age or the sex breakdown. It draws on American veterans referred for a clinically indicated treadmill test, and sibling analyses that do publish demographics run about ninety-three to ninety-four per cent male, mean ages in the sixties.
So older male veterans sent for a cardiac stress test.
And barely a cohort of women at all. Third, the least-fit quintile is substantially populated by people already ill — reverse causation, not a dose of exercise not taken.

The statistic the headlines will skip. Adding the best-regarded physiological predictor of death to standard risk factors moved the discrimination statistic from zero point six six two to zero point six eight two. A gain of two hundredths.
[thoughtful] It matters. It isn't magic.
The Diary. Thirteen of sixteen events publish no price at all. The arts-council festivals print theirs; the promoters and sports bodies have moved theirs behind a button.
[curious] One deadline this week?

Sunday the eighteenth, when the Singapore Writers Festival early bird ends and twenty-four dollars becomes thirty. And one in December — Friday the fifth, when Grand Sumo's January tournament opens advance sales. November sold out on all fifteen days.

The one worth the trip has not quite opened. Osteria Da Su, the NAE:UM Group's new room on Telok Ayer Street, running Korean ingredients through Italian technique under Chef Suji Park. About sixty to seventy-five dollars for three courses.
[amused] And the queue story?
Tokyo Onigiri, in the basement of One Raffles Place, open since Monday. Eighteen fillings, classics at four ninety. Waits rose from about thirty minutes on opening day to about sixty.

Eleven sharp, or Saturday. And two returns with real pegs — Noci Bakehouse has a second outlet at Orchard Gateway leading on panuozzo, and Food Opera under ION reopened in late September, re-tenanted around heritage names.
The Long Read. Kyrgyzstan — a law in force this month wires whether you voted into the pension file.
[gasps] Say that again.

Law number one three six, passed in three readings in June and signed in July. It moves presidential elections from Sunday to the fourth Wednesday of January — the next is the twenty-seventh. And it counts that day in the insurance record, the ledger that decides your pension.
Conditional on what?
On confirmation that he or she voted. Without a valid excuse, the Wednesday becomes an unpaid non-working day.
[curious] And who confirms it?
Not you. The Social Fund pulls participation data from the election commission through Tündük — the state's data-exchange layer, named after the wooden crown that caps a yurt and sits on the flag.

The confirmation lands in two places. In payroll, where an employer must distinguish between staff who voted and staff who did not. And in the pension file, where the draft adds it to the documents used for awarding a pension, recalculating one, and paying the funeral benefit.

The average monthly wage was fifty-one thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight som over the first five months of this year — about twenty-seven US dollars a day. One voting day is forty-six thousandths of one per cent of the current minimum record.
[scoffs] So fifteen elections across forty adult years buys about three working weeks of pension credit.
And it can't reach most people. Sixty-six per cent of the employed are informal on the Social Fund's own count. A bazaar trader has no average daily earnings to preserve.
[thoughtful] So what is it for?

The incentive isn't the product. The register is. The law's real output is a permanent, machine-readable, per-citizen attribute — voted, or did not — held by the social-insurance system, already cross-referenced to employment and civil status.
[curious] Is there a precedent?

There is, and it isn't Central Asian. Bolivia has issued a certificate of suffrage since long before anyone had an interface — valid for ninety days, and in that window the state and the banks ask for it. In March its migration service made it a condition of a passport.
[curious] And the difference?

The certificate was a document you carried. Tündük is a request between two computers. Latin America made the citizen prove participation at a counter. Central Asia makes the pension fund ask the election commission, silently, and write the answer into the file.

And the counter-authority is already written down, quoted by the OSCE in the same report. The Venice Commission's code says that since abstention may indicate a political choice, lists of persons voting should not be published.

It is now monetising them. That's the claim — not that a country has made voting compulsory. Several have, openly, for a century. But that this is the first case in the former Soviet space of a state turning that forbidden list into a line item in the social-insurance ledger.
[skeptical] Will it work?

Probably — and that's the deeper irony, because working will prove nothing. Turnout at the last parliamentary election was thirty-six point nine per cent. The OSCE found that campaign restrictive, vote-buying allegations wide-spread, and the count negatively assessed in over a third of observed stations.
So when turnout rises in January?
The state will read it as consent restored. It will be the price of a Wednesday.
The Last Word — and a note about this issue. No spine.
[curious] None at all?

Three editions running have threaded one idea through twelve desks, and the reader starts to see the machine. This one is a straight news book. But one page is worth sitting with, and it's the local one.

Singapore published a response ladder whose first rung is a twenty-four-hour reading above two hundred. For six weeks the reading never got there. On Tuesday it topped out at a hundred and sixty-eight — and the masks went out anyway.
[thoughtful] Which was the right call.

And also an admission. A twenty-four-hour average is designed to be stable, which is another way of saying it's designed to be late. Smoke that arrives on a Tuesday afternoon is fully visible in it on Wednesday night.
[thoughtful] So the ladder wasn't too high.
It was pinned to the wrong clock. A published rung is a promise: here is what we will do, and here is when, so you need not trust our judgement in the moment.
It's a rung attached to an instrument that can see an afternoon, published in advance, so that the discretion exercised this week never has to be exercised unannounced again.
[warmly] That's a good one to carry around all day.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
